If God’s relation of knowledge were not also a relation of bringing existence into being, He could not know Himself as the source of every existence. Knowing Himself would require knowing every existence before it occurs, so the relation of knowledge would be present before its object existed, while the creative relation would not yet be present. That is impossible. The divine realm of knowledge therefore includes both what already exists and what can exist.

The knowing and acting powers are inseparable for two reasons. First, one cannot be lost while the other remains, unlike perception and movement in animals: sight may fail while movement remains, or the reverse. Second, the two human powers do not have separate bodily locations, unlike animal perception, mostly in the head, and movement, in the muscles.

Some judgments need no learning, such as that justice is good and injustice bad. Others depend on custom or reasoning, such as whether killing animals is wrong. To decide to tell a particular truth, a person may reason: this is true; every truth is just; therefore this is just; every just thing is good; and every good thing should be done; so this truth should be told. The practical intellect does not directly carry out good acts. If action means ability, that is opposed to knowledge; if it means movement, it is an animal power, not an intellect. The practical intellect is a more distant source of action and a direct source of knowledge about how to act. It guides the powers of desire and movement. The Second Teacher, al-Fārābī, says that theoretical intellect lets a person know what they cannot do, while practical intellect lets them know what they can do by choice.

The three senses differ in how far they are from one another. The first concerns a power to perceive, as with the potential theoretical intellect; the second concerns actual perception, as with intellect in act; and the third concerns action.
This is a rhetorical argument: if even the lower level is called intellect, surely this higher one deserves the name.
“First principles” here means the basic starting points, as opposed to conclusions, not all self-evident truths.

Another reading, perhaps better, is that “intellect in habit” contrasts with a mere capacity or absence. The potential intellect is only a capacity; the second intellect already possesses first principles and their actuality. Avicenna discusses it in The Origin and Return.

This means recognizing the Active Intellect through direct encounter, not merely learning about it. Direct knowledge is the highest kind, and seeing the forms within it cannot be separated from encountering it.

“Intellect” may mean the soul itself, one of its levels, or one of its powers; in every case it is either a power or an act of knowing. The potential intellect may be understood as the first appearance of the rational soul, like embers already present in coal before it catches fire. It is then the soul at a certain level. Or it may be understood as one of the soul’s powers, just as the rational soul has theoretical and practical powers, and the animal soul has powers of perception and movement. The theoretical power itself has the four levels just listed.

The potential intellect may be understood as a readiness close to completion—the intellect in habit—or as a readiness that still needs teaching and preparation, such as intuitive or sacred insight. The wording can also be read as “prepared,” in the passive sense.
“All things” may mean everything in every realm, including the divine realm and the world of names and attributes, most of which has no matter. Or it may mean all things in the natural world.
If we consider the existence of the forms, they are one form, because all exist through the one existence of the soul. If we consider their different essences, they are many forms.

The word “intelligible” is derived from “intellect,” hinting that the knower and what is known are one. It is like calling two things “lover” and “beloved” from the same root, or calling something “ensouled” from the word “soul.”

The comparison with lines or figures pressed into wax suggests that intelligibles extend through the whole subject, not just across its surface. The Second Teacher seems to mean the other subjects in which figures are formed. In a note, the author says that the analogy may concern only shapes and arrangements on the body’s surface, since natural forms extend through the body’s depth. The point may be that the distinction between form and matter becomes less clear in intellectual things, and perhaps even in bodily things.

This differs from the earlier comparison: there the pattern spreads through the matter, while here it is treated as identical with the matter. “Figure” here may mean one of the qualities tied to quantity: straightness or curvature, evenness or oddness, shape or angle, or a shape combined with color.

The clearer reading would omit the word “not,” though it appears in the manuscripts. It can be explained by taking the sentence to mean that forms become actual only when they are present throughout the wax-like subject, not merely on its surface. Another possible reading treats the word as a passive form of “to resemble.”

The three descriptions refer to the same single meaning: the form understood may be called actual knower, actual intellect, or actual intelligible; the one who understands may likewise be called by any of these names. The same applies to the intellect itself.

The features may be separable from the form in different instances or at different levels. Some, such as place and position, can vary by subject: the outermost sphere has no place in the usual sense, but it does have an order and position. Quantity and shape, however, cannot be separated from their subject. Most features cannot be separated from one another.

“Where” has levels: being somewhere in general, being in a particular country, being in a house within that country, and being in a particular room of that house. These all count as “where” in the ordinary sense, but the general concept of “where” is distinct from any one specific place.

Read “understands” in the active sense, following the doctrine that knower and known are one in existence, not in meaning. An essence without existence cannot be established, much less be an intellect and intelligible. The existence of what is understood is the very existence of the knower. It becomes actual intellect because it is free from matter, time, and place, and has a wider, more unified existence. A particular fire known through sense or imagination is confined by time and place. Once understood intellectually, it exists in a single, encompassing way that includes every particular fire—past, future, and in the next life. To know the universal fire is to know all its fine details. This is why the universal can both bring knowledge and be known, while the particular cannot do so in the same way.
Before that, the person was “nothing worth mentioning,” as the Qur'an says: “Has there not come upon man a period of time when he was nothing worth mentioning?”

When the actual intellect, which completes other intellects, understands itself, this also points to its union with the Active Intellect. A saying attributed to the Prophet teaches: “Know God through God, and the messenger through the message.”
This means universal intellects that are separate from matter by their nature, not because someone has abstracted them from matter.

The passage can be read in two ways. It may mean that the intellect understands those forms as forms, without needing to abstract them anew; or that it understands the separate intellect itself in the way it understands itself, with the intellect as knower and the forms as what it knows. The first reading is clearer. Another grammatical reading is also possible: the separate intellect encounters forms already within itself, just as it encounters itself. In every case, the point is that forms that never existed in matter do not need to be abstracted from matter.
These forms have no material subject, but their existence in us differs in completeness from their existence in themselves. Their presence in us is limited by our capacity to receive them.
This is the actual intellect that is our own being; what is present in us as its content is the intelligibles themselves.
The Arabic can be read with either a kasra or a fatḥa on the relevant letter, giving two grammatical readings.

Philosophers disagree about whether the acquired intellect can arise while the soul is still occupied with managing the body. The commentator holds that it can. For some people who know God, the body is like a garment they can put on and take off. A simple intellect whose dominant element is itself may have no awareness except the highest kind: the simple intellect, which contains all intelligibles in one unified reality. It can know them all at once, beyond time. The commentator then cites Rumi: “The pure ones’ bodies became pure spirit; their words, their breath, their very form—all became the absolute, unmarked spirit.”
The rising and descending levels of existence form a cycle: nature rises toward intellect, and intellect descends toward nature, without losing what it has attained.
Alexander’s account leaves out the acquired intellect, just as some accounts leave out the intellect in habit. The author discusses the substance of this treatise in Keys to the Unseen.

“Potential” here means pure possibility without any actuality mixed into it. Prime matter is all things in pure possibility; likewise, the potential intellect is pure potential. It is a simple substance whose kind and distinguishing feature are interwoven.
The Arabic construction means “so that it may become,” with a preposition omitted in a regular grammatical pattern.

The “will” is emphatic, not a reference to the future. If the intellect already had a particular intellectual form that resisted other forms, those actual forms would clash, as they would in prime matter, and it could not receive every form.

Each sense is like matter for the things it perceives, so it must be free of those particular things. Otherwise, it would perceive them mixed with its own state. The statement that the senses do not perceive their objects in themselves means that those objects are absent from the senses’ own subject. A sense must be like its object in the way matter is suited to its form, as a seed is suited to a plant, an egg to a chick, and a seed of life to an animal. Sight is suited to colors and light, hearing to sound, and so on. The potential intellect is similarly suited to universal forms. This likeness does not mean that the perceiver already contains one of the forms it perceives; that would contradict the need to be free of it.

The reference is to the “vital spirit” of the body. Each power has this spirit as its subject, like a form in matter, and the power’s subject is itself like matter for what it perceives. Taste, for example, depends on the saliva that serves as its instrument. That moisture must also be receptive, or it could not taste flavors in their pure state.

This answers an apparent objection: if touch does not sense what resembles its own heat or cold, it seems to have admitted that the sense is not free of what it perceives. A body made of elements cannot be free of all basic sensible qualities, but it is free of the particular qualities it perceives—either because they are stronger or weaker than what is in the body.

Two things prevent a power from finding its objects within itself. First, an existing form blocks another form, since what is already actual cannot receive actuality in the same respect; a receptive power must first be open, then take on a form. Second, without this openness, there can be no distinction between the power and the object. The intellect’s ability to distinguish is not like the saliva’s ability to distinguish tastes.
Every actual existent is preceded by possibility.

Perceptive powers are bodily powers spread through the vital spirits in the brain and the cavities of the nerves. They do not perceive themselves, but perceive what is absent from them; each has a limited range of objects, and so is both limited in power and actual in its own way. The potential intellect differs: because it can understand everything, it must be free of all those forms.

Just as knowledge in act is one with what is known in act, the actual knower and actual intellect are one with what is understood in act. The intelligible is therefore actual intellect and actual knower.

Having discussed the Active Intellect’s role in knowledge, Alexander turns to its role in action. It may govern the elemental world directly, returning things to their higher intellectual levels, as a steward is sometimes said to do; or it may govern through the motions of the heavens; or it may act through nature, which combines and separates the elements. These possibilities are not mutually exclusive. If we see natural powers as levels of the Active Intellect’s agency, it acts alone; if we focus on the different levels, we include the other causes as well. Some might think these lowly things and actions unworthy of the Active Intellect, but the commentator rejects that view. All its acts are wise and exact. In general, intellect and providence guide this world, as the other intellects complete the souls of the heavenly bodies. The commentator suspects that a copyist changed “intellectual levels” to “divine bodies.”
That is, through greater or lesser nearness.

This note clarifies the pronouns in Alexander’s sentence. “Whether we can understand” concerns the soul; “nor is it our work” concerns the intellect. “When we come to be” means that the Active Intellect is naturally present in us from the beginning, giving the potential intellect its foundation and the actual intellect its actuality.

This points to the union of knower and known. The knower is not a place in which the known is lodged; it changes into the intelligibles, as matter changes into forms. The sense power likewise becomes one with the forms it senses.

A natural kind is a unified whole. The difficulty is that the soul’s distinguishing feature makes it a definite form in the human being, so how can it become something indeterminate? Elsewhere, a plant becomes an animal through indeterminate matter. Also, if the soul is the body’s form, how can it become identical with what is separate from the body? And if soul and intellect are distinct kinds, how can one become the other?

Essence brings limitation and difference; existence brings breadth and identity. The essences of green, indigo, and deep black differ, but their existence is one continuous reality with degrees. Its continuous unity is the unity of one individual.

For example, a body may be potentially white and actually something else at the same time. Or a body may be actual through its bodily form and potential for motion, as philosophers argue when they establish prime matter. An intellectual being, too, may have one perfection in act and another in potentiality.

A body is actual through its form and receptive to motion through its matter, which carries potentiality. The soul is different: the very soul that is actual as a soul is also potential to receive an intellectual form. The note then offers several ways to understand this.

The potential intellect is not prime matter in the strict sense. Strictly speaking, matter is a natural subject that carries another natural form, and both remain together in one natural level. The soul does not remain unchanged when it becomes intellect in act, just as a sensible natural form does not remain in the same way when it becomes an intelligible. The earlier form gives way to the later one, as the earthly and heavenly worlds are transformed in the next life. So the potential intellect is like matter for the intellectual world, not a material subject that remains alongside its new form. The Second Teacher likewise calls actual intellect a kind of matter for the acquired intellect.

Potentiality in a material subject means that, at one time, the thing is without the form it is ready to receive, and later receives it. This kind of potentiality does not apply to immaterial realities: an intelligible such as universal fire has an encompassing existence beyond time and place. Thus, to say that the potential intellect becomes actual does not mean that one separate thing receives another. It means that a single, continuous reality develops through connected levels.

If the potential intellect has learned first principles yet remains able to know other things, this does not require a second subject. The “potentiality” means that it is receptive to further knowledge. The intellect also has levels: one level may have become a particular intelligible while another has not, as portions of prime matter can become different things. Another possible answer is that the soul has real actuality and potentiality without being made of two parts: its actuality is its own, while its potentiality comes from its relation to the body, which is the soul’s matter. As it takes on intelligibles in succession, the body’s potentiality is involved in a corresponding succession.

A further answer accepts composition, but not of prime matter and bodily form. It is a composition of potential intellect and separate intellectual form, each at its own level. This also helps explain the “Muḥammadan Reality” in the mystical tradition, said to rise in its ascent beyond the Active Intellect. The universal intellects are complete in themselves, but the prophetic spirit is joined to bodily matter, which makes further transformation possible while the body remains. There is therefore a difference between the Active Intellect considered apart from natural existence and the Active Intellect as it meets natural existence. The latter can continue to rise as far as God wills.
This means the form itself, not a mental image of it.
Something mixed with other things is not pure or unrestricted.

A wording note: the text can be read as saying that “being present to something able to understand” is part of what it means to understand, rather than being the whole meaning. The author leaves the other part of the definition open because the argument does not need it.
This argument concerns intellect in act that was once potential, not an intellect that is actual by nature from the start.
The form being discussed is the first form that makes the potential intellect actual. A natural kind becomes actual through one of its individuals.
This is the form that was first only possible. The first form is present at the level of potentiality; it cannot already be an unrelated form that is actual by nature.
A part counts as a separate part only in relation to the whole. The parts are gathered together by their shared arrangement.

This would turn potentiality into another potentiality: the part like form would become the receptive part, and the part like matter would become the form. It also leaves no role for the matter-like part, since the form-like part would already understand.
If one part can understand both parts, it is already the actual intellect; the other part does not help make the whole actual.
The reverse arrangement fails in the same way.

The author’s list may include understanding the whole through itself. If this means direct knowledge, the whole is one with what it knows, which supports the author’s point. If it means knowledge through a mental image, the same difficulty returns. The two wholes may be arranged alike or differently, but either way the argument returns to one of the failed options.

I say: Avicenna's purpose is to state what understanding means, not to give its ultimate cause. His words, "by a further form coming to exist in the potential intellect," make this clear. Nor does he reject the causal explanation merely because it would explain a thing through itself. The difficulty is that a form can exist in something receptive without being understood: this is true of a form in matter. If we add that the form must be intelligible, we are left asking what makes it intelligible in the first place.

The commentator offers another explanation: the potential intellect understands the form because it receives it as an immaterial reality in an immaterial being. This adds a third possibility to Avicenna’s choice.
Avicenna does not accept change from one substance into another. In particular, he does not accept that a nonmaterial substance can change its very nature.

Avicenna counts only ten separate intellects. The Illuminationists allow a complete guiding light to join the ranks of the separate lights after its bodily shell is left behind, but Avicenna does not accept separate intellects of the same level.

The soul begins through the body and continues as a spirit after death. The potential intellect is not a separate being that already knows itself as the argument requires. One possible reply is that “potential intellect” means a power to understand, or the soul after it has reached the level of intellect in habit.
Another reading is that, without the first principle, the other part would have to be both present and absent.
“Equal” here does not mean equal in size or in how many things a statement fits. It means sharing the same kind, as two people do. The rule applies to that kind of equality.

Other truths depend on the first principle through a simple argument: assume either the principle or its opposite, then rule out one side to establish the other. But the first principle does not break down into ordinary statements with a subject and a predicate. It is a basic choice between affirmation and denial.

The author points out that, before judgment, the idea of existence is the clearest starting point in thought. It also points to real existence, which comes before every particular kind of reality. Its meaning is clearer than any other basic idea; it is the end of the chain of what is self-evident, just as the Necessary Being is the end of the chain of what depends on something else.

Studying geometry, arithmetic, and logic helps in two ways: it teaches someone to check whether a proof works, and it gives practice in certainty. Many basic questions are self-evident, but people need to become used to recognizing them.

You may ask: Is the point simply that whatever is free of matter knows itself, since a body or a bodily thing does not? That conclusion does not follow merely by reversing the statement. From "everything that knows itself is nonbodily" we cannot infer that everything nonbodily knows itself; at most, an affirmative statement gives us a conclusion about some such things. I reply: The contrast with bodies may be given because we learn what things are through their opposites. It can also form a fuller argument: no body or bodily thing knows itself, and nothing wholly separate from matter is bodily. From these two premises we reach the intended result: nothing separate from matter fails to know itself. The further statement, "Every nonbodily being ...," offers another route to the conclusion. It applies to a rational soul, a separate intellect, the Necessary Being, and—if the knower truly becomes one with what it knows—to the form through which another thing is understood.

The first and second methods may be one argument stated in two ways. In any case, they strongly support the claim that separate substances know themselves. The philosophers focus on substances because an intellectual form is free of matter and potentiality. A form that exists in itself is present to itself; presence is what makes it known. The same existence that makes it present also makes it a knower.
Read “he said” as the reply to “when he had shown.”

Avicenna does not explicitly say that a form becomes one with the thing it makes actual. The commentator reads “present to it” as union, much as existence is present to existence or unity to what is one. The proof works without that reading: if a form makes another thing an actual intellect by being present to it, then a form that exists by itself is an intellect and knower in its own right.

This is the second argument. The first describes knowledge as a thing’s not being hidden from itself; the second describes it as being present to itself. “Not hidden” is more exact because “presence” sounds like a relation between two separate things.
The point is that a separate being may exist in itself without being present to something else. This is different from a thing that exists through another thing.

One might object that the author assumes the soul is separate before proving that every separate being understands itself. But he uses only the fact that we know ourselves, not that we are separate. Knowing oneself means one and the same self is both knower and known. Even an animal knows itself in a direct way because it seeks what suits it and avoids what harms it. The author’s claim about intellect is stronger: the soul understands itself as intellect, not merely through imagination or instinct.

Philosophers hold three views about how the soul knows particular things. One says the soul knows only universals; its powers know particulars, and we speak loosely when we say “the soul knows.” Another says the soul itself knows particulars through powers that are levels of the soul; this is the author’s view. A third says the soul knows particulars directly, while its powers serve as instruments. The commentator reads Suhrawardī as agreeing with the second view, not the first. The author’s criticism is that the two earlier philosophers reject the claim that the powers are levels of the soul when they explain how particulars are known. For universals, the author says the soul knows them through union with their kinds, not by looking at them from a distance.

God is the Light of lights. The only reason we cannot fully understand Him is that our limited minds cannot encompass the Necessary Being. In one sense, all things reveal Him, because each has a side turned toward the light of existence and a side marked by its own limits. Existence is light; concealment is darkness. We can know God through His attributes, which are easier to understand than His full reality. We can speak of Him through existence, light, awareness, life, unity, and love. We can also know Him directly when the self is overcome by His presence. These are ways of knowing the Necessary Being, especially when we see that our light is borrowed from Him.

The objection assumes that God has an essence that can be defined. The commentator says it is the reverse: we cannot fully grasp God’s real existence, but we can define the ordinary essence of a possible thing.

The commentator sharply criticizes al-Rāzī for confusing the shared concept of existence with real existence itself. When philosophers say God is pure existence, they mean real existence, which drives away nonexistence—not the general idea of “existence.” When they say His essence is His existence, they mean He is existence in its fullest degree, untouched by essence as a limit. This does not mean that existence in general is the Necessary Being. The levels of existence differ in completeness, and cause and effect share a connection of kind: lower levels are contained in higher ones.

This argument may be intended for philosophers in Aristotle’s school, who say that knowledge of other things comes through forms in the mind. They want to show how a separate being can know another thing. If it can be joined to another intelligible form, the image must be that form itself. But it is difficult to argue that this possibility belongs to the form’s nature. A simpler argument would be that a separate being can be present with another separate being, or that a cause and its effect are necessarily joined. Those arguments rely on direct knowledge rather than mental forms.

The main point is that separate intellects do not have knowledge through mental copies. Our own learned knowledge works differently. We directly experience immaterial forms, then, because we are also connected to matter, we compare those forms with what we see in the material world. We then form ideas and concepts such as “horse” or “tree.” This is how knowledge through mental ideas arises. Pure intellects have no such link to matter, so they do not form ideas that stand apart from existence. They know things directly, through the existence of those things themselves.
The shared kind must apply equally to every member, not by degrees. The argument does not work for a kind whose members have different levels of completeness.
This leaves open the possibility that the same kind can exist in different ways, even if its essential features remain the same.

The relation between two ideas within a mind is different from the relation between a separate being and an idea present to it. One is like two features sharing one subject; the other is like a feature and its subject. If the argument is only about images in the mind, that may avoid the problem of having a thing’s possibility depend on its already existing. The two claims concern the same moment, not one depending on the other over time.

If the argument uses a specific kind of being together, one could say it is only a feature of the mind. If it uses “being together” in the broadest sense, that broad relation does not prove that every specific kind of relation is possible. A physical form and an immaterial form, for example, cannot be together in the same way.

The first “together with” refers to what is joined; the second to what it is joined with. God cannot be joined to another thing as one item beside another. His togetherness with things means that He sustains them, not that He shares a place or relation with them.

The conclusion is even harder if applied to all separate beings, including God. If God could be together with every intelligible form at once, He would have an unlimited number of distinct aspects. The argument says such forms must be joined without order, unless another proof establishes a cause-and-effect order.

The argument may establish only that such a relation is possible. It does not, by itself, prove knowledge. To establish knowledge, one must also show that there is no barrier between two immaterial beings, such as the light-like existence of one being present to another.
This means that intellect is the union of the knower and what is known. The commentator says this is the very claim the argument was supposed to prove, so using it here assumes the conclusion.
What is understood in act is itself intellect in act, and it makes the being that receives it an actual intellect.

This refers to the first premise of the fourth argument: any separate being can be understood by another. If it can be understood in act, it must be understood by something. But in the separate world, possibility is never left waiting to become actual. Since a being understands everything it can understand, and this includes itself, it understands itself.

If “intellect in act” means an actual intelligible form, as in Farabi’s account, then there is no problem: the human soul always has at least one basic intelligible idea. But the objection means intellect in act in the stronger sense of the Active Intellect, or at least the third stage of the soul’s intellect. Avicenna’s account of separation includes freedom from time, place, direction, and potentiality, so the problem remains if the soul is separate from its first moment.
Bodily makeup may give the soul a good power of reasoning, quick insight, or sacred insight. The soul’s actions may also grow stronger through practice and good habits.

One reply is that being separate by nature does not make the soul an actual intellect from the start. In Avicenna’s view, the soul’s knowledge of particular things is a later perfection. It depends on earlier sense and imagination, which prepare the soul to form universal intellectual ideas. So the soul’s existence as a separate substance does not mean that all its intellectual powers are already actual.
